summary: This specification defines a TLS handshake message for exchanging supplemental application data. Hello message extensions determine which supplemental data types both client and server support, and the new message carries the data. Other documents define the specific types. It updates RFC 4346 and was later updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4680 adds one TLS handshake message for extra data used by applications above TLS. The client and server first agree on the kinds of data they support, then send the agreed data in that message.

subtitle: Defines a TLS handshake message for application data negotiated by the client and server.

tldr.problem: Applications sometimes need to exchange extra data during a TLS handshake, and separate handshake messages for each data type would multiply message formats.
tldr.mechanism: The peers negotiate supported data types in TLS hello extensions, then carry agreed data in a supplemental_data handshake message.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the container, not individual data types. It updates RFC 4346 and was later updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4680 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2006. It updates RFC 4346 and has been updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996.

sections.title: Why TLS Needs Supplemental Data
sections.content:
Some applications need data during TLS setup to help with authentication or authorization decisions. Examples in the RFC include a user-name hint for locating credentials and assertions used for authorization.

Rather than define a separate handshake message for each application need, RFC 4680 defines one message that carries a list of supplemental data entries. TLS itself does not interpret this data; it is intended for applications and protocols above TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications may need extra information while a secure connection is being established. This RFC defines one TLS message that can carry different kinds of agreed application data.

sections.title: The supplemental_data Message
sections.content:
The new handshake message is named supplemental_data and has message type 23. Its body contains one or more entries. Each entry has a data-type identifier, a 16-bit length and data whose format depends on that type.

This RFC defines the container but no actual data types. Other specifications define each type, its syntax and processing, and the TLS hello extensions used to negotiate it. If a supplemental-data message appears, it MUST contain a non-empty entry for at least one defined type.
sections.plainLanguage: The message contains entries with a type, a length and the data. Other specifications define what each type means and how an application processes it.

sections.title: Agreeing Before Sending Data
sections.content:
The client and server MUST explicitly agree on each supplemental-data type through extensions in their hello messages. A sender MUST NOT send a data type that the peers did not negotiate.

Each side can send at most one SupplementalData message. A duplicate message or a message sent without agreement is a fatal error, and the receiver MUST close the connection with an unexpected_message alert.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers announce which data types they support in their hello messages. A receiver closes the connection if it gets an unnegotiated or duplicate supplemental-data message.

sections.title: Where the Message Appears
sections.content:
If used, SupplementalData MUST be the first handshake message after the hello messages. The server sends it immediately after ServerHello and before Certificate. The client sends it before its Certificate.

The message can travel from client to server, from server to client, or in both directions. The data is optional and depends on the negotiated application data types.
sections.plainLanguage: When present, supplemental data comes immediately after the hello messages and before certificate messages. Either side can send it, depending on the negotiated type.

sections.title: Protecting Sensitive Supplemental Data
sections.content:
Each supplemental-data type has its own security considerations, which its defining document must explain. The position of the message means a server can send its supplemental data before it has authenticated the client.

For sensitive data, the RFC describes a double handshake: first establish protected communication, then perform a second handshake inside that protection and exchange supplemental data after both sides are authenticated. Messages in the second handshake are protected by both TLS sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: A server may otherwise send supplemental data before it knows who the client is. For sensitive data, the RFC describes a second handshake inside an already protected session.

sections.title: Handshake and Data-Type Registries
sections.content:
IANA added supplemental_data(23) to the TLS HandshakeType registry and created a registry for TLS Supplemental Data Formats.

The RFC assigns data-type values from 0 through 16385 by Standards Action, 16386 through 65279 by IETF Consensus, and 65280 through 65535 for Private Use.
sections.plainLanguage: Registries reserve a handshake number for the new message and organize numbers for future supplemental-data types. Different number ranges use different assignment rules.
